assignment.title: Radical Expressions — Honors
assignment.essentialQuestion: Why can it be useful to simplify expressions?
assignment.teacherNotes: Honors version of Bluebonnet Algebra II — Radicals, Lesson 2 (Operations with Radical Expressions), TEKS A2.7G. Beyond the regular lesson: higher even and odd indices with absolute value decided and explained, binomial and two-radical denominators, cube-root denominators, radical zeros of quadratics and their conjugates, nested radicals, a counterexample to √(a + b) = √a + √b, comparisons without a calculator, the golden ratio, and Heron’s formula. “Simplify” answers are graded by value AND form: any arrangement of the simplified expression is accepted; the expression retyped, a perfect power left under a radical, a radical left in a denominator, missing absolute value bars, or a calculator decimal are marked not yet. Practice includes two audited SAT items (MathMaster CCMR bank). Warm-Up and DOL are generated per student and back Recovery.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[3]{ {{R}} a^{ {{e}} } }$.
hints: Find the largest perfect cube that divides {{R}}.
Split a^{{e}} into a power whose exponent is a multiple of 3, times a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. ∛(a⁶) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Take the cube root of the perfect-cube factor.
solutionReview.commonError: Taking a square root of the powers instead of a cube root: ∛(a^{{e3}}) is a^{{m}}.

hints: The factors are conjugates: (u + v)(u − v) = u² − v².
Square the radical term: the coefficient and the radical are both squared.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (u + v)(u − v) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Conjugates multiply to a difference of squares.
reasoning: (u + v)(u − v) = u² − v² with u = {{a}}√{{b}} and v = {{c}}.
So the product is {{a2b}} − {{c2}} = {{v}}: no radical is left.
solutionReview.commonError: Squaring only the whole-number part: (a√b)² = a² · b, so the radical part squares too.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{x^2 {{tc|xterm}} + {{c2}}}$. The variable $x$ can be any real number.
hints: Is the radicand a perfect square trinomial?
For any real number u, √(u²) = |u|.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √((−3)²) equals…

solutionReview.headline: A perfect square under a square root gives an absolute value.
reasoning: √((x {{c|signed}})²) = |x {{c|signed}}|, because a square root is never negative.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing x {{c|signed}} without bars: when x {{c|signed}} is negative, the square root is still positive.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[4]{162x^9y^{12}}$. Use absolute value bars only where they are needed.

responses.label: Why does y³ need absolute value bars but x² does not?
options: y may be negative, so y³ may be negative, but a fourth root is never negative; x² is never negative
Every variable outside an even root needs bars
x² needs bars too, because x may be negative
responses.answer: y may be negative, so y³ may be negative, but a fourth root is never negative; x² is never negative

steps.title: Product and Quotient Properties
steps.instruction: ⁿ√(ab) = ⁿ√a · ⁿ√b and ⁿ√(a/b) = ⁿ√a / ⁿ√b when the roots are real. Split the radicand into an nth-power factor and what is left.

steps.title: Even and odd roots
steps.instruction: For an even index, ⁿ√(aⁿ) = |a|: an even root is never negative. For an odd index, ⁿ√(aⁿ) = a: an odd root keeps the sign.

steps.title: Simplest radical form
steps.instruction: Smallest index; no nth-power factor left in a radicand; no fraction under a radical; no radical in a denominator; like radicals combined.

hints: 162 = 81 · 2, and 81 is a fourth power.
x⁹ = x⁸ · x, and y¹² is the fourth power of y³.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For an even index n, ⁿ√(aⁿ) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Pull out the fourth powers, then decide on the bars.
reasoning: 2x stays under the radical (so x ≥ 0 there).
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 3x²y³∜(2x): y may be negative, which makes y³ negative, but a fourth root never is.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[5]{-64a^{11}b^5}$.

responses.label: Why are there no absolute value bars in this answer?
options: The index 5 is odd, and an odd root keeps the sign of the radicand
Because a and b are positive
Absolute value bars are never used with roots
responses.answer: The index 5 is odd, and an odd root keeps the sign of the radicand

hints: −64 = (−32) · 2, and −32 is a fifth power.
a¹¹ = a¹⁰ · a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. ⁵√(−32) equals…

solutionReview.headline: An odd root keeps the sign.
reasoning: ⁵√((−2a²b)⁵) = −2a²b, so the expression is −2a²b ⁵√(2a).
solutionReview.commonError: Dropping the negative sign or adding bars: an odd root keeps the sign of the radicand, so neither is right.

questions.prompt: Rationalize a binomial denominator: simplify $\dfrac{3 + \sqrt{2}}{2 - \sqrt{2}}$.

responses.label: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by

steps.title: Conjugates
steps.instruction: a + √b and a − √b are conjugates: (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b, with no radical left.

steps.title: Rationalize a binomial denominator
steps.instruction: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. Example: 1/(3 + √5) · (3 − √5)/(3 − √5) = (3 − √5)/4.

hints: The conjugate of a − √b is a + √b.
A conjugate pair multiplies to a difference of squares, with no radical left.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (a − √b)(a + √b) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by √2/√2: the denominator becomes 2√2 − 2, which still has a radical.

questions.prompt: Two radicals in the denominator. Simplify $\dfrac{\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{3}}$.

responses.label: After multiplying by the conjugate, the denominator is

hints: Square the numerator by multiplying it by itself (FOIL).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (√u − √v)(√u + √v) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Conjugate, then reduce the fraction.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at (8 + 2√15)/2: every term has a common factor of 2.

questions.prompt: Cube roots in denominators. Simplify $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt[3]{4}}$ and $\dfrac{5}{\sqrt[3]{9x}}$: multiply by the cube root that makes each denominator’s radicand a perfect cube.

steps.title: Rationalizing a cube root
steps.instruction: Multiply by the cube root that turns the radicand into a perfect cube. Example: 1/∛5 · ∛25/∛25 = ∛25/∛125 = ∛25/5.

hints: Ask what ∛4 must be multiplied by to give a perfect cube under the radical.
For 9x, you need 27x³ under the radical.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A cube root in a denominator is gone when its radicand is…

solutionReview.headline: Complete the perfect cube.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by ∛4/∛4: 4 · 4 = 16 is not a perfect cube.

questions.prompt: Radicals as zeros. Show that $2 + \sqrt{3}$ is a zero of $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1$, then find the other zero and match each exact zero to an x-intercept of the graph.

responses.label: On the graph, which x-intercept is the zero you substituted?
options: Neither: exact radical zeros do not show on a graph

hints: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².
Add the three parts: (2 + √3)² − 4(2 + √3) + 1.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (√3)² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute, simplify, and use the conjugate.
reasoning: Irrational zeros of a polynomial with integer coefficients come in conjugate pairs, so 2 − √3 is the other zero: the zeros add to 4 and multiply to 4 − 3 = 1.
Since √3 ≈ 1.73, 2 + √3 ≈ 3.73 and 2 − √3 ≈ 0.27: the two x-intercepts on the graph.
solutionReview.commonError: Squaring 2 + √3 as 4 + 3: (2 + √3)² also has the middle term 2 · 2 · √3 = 4√3.

questions.prompt: Challenge: a nested radical. Find positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $\sqrt{7 + 4\sqrt{3}} = a + \sqrt{b}$. Square both sides and match the parts.
hints: Expand (a + √b)².
Match the parts: the whole-number parts must be equal, and so must the radical parts.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (a + √b)² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Square, then match the rational and irrational parts.
reasoning: 2a√b = 4√3 gives a√b = 2√3, so a = 2 and b = 3.
solutionReview.commonError: Matching a + √b to 7 + 4√3 directly: square a + √b first, then match the parts.

questions.prompt: Error analysis. A classmate writes $\sqrt{a + b} = \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$. Test the rule with numbers, then decide what is true.

responses.label: So √(a + b) = √a + √b is…
options: false in general: a = 9, b = 16 is a counterexample
true whenever a and b are perfect squares
responses.answer: false in general: a = 9, b = 16 is a counterexample

responses.label: Which IS true for all a, b ≥ 0?
So √(x² + 9) simplifies to…
options: Nothing simpler: it is not x + 3
responses.answer: Nothing simpler: it is not x + 3

hints: Evaluate both sides with a = 9 and b = 16.
A rule is an identity only if it works for every allowed value.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. How many counterexamples does it take to show a rule is false?

solutionReview.headline: One counterexample breaks a rule.
reasoning: So √(a + b) = √a + √b is not an identity.
The Product Property √(ab) = √a · √b is true for a, b ≥ 0.
So √(x² + 9) cannot be split into √(x²) + √9: it is already as simple as it gets.
solutionReview.commonError: Splitting a root over a sum: √(a + b) is not √a + √b, though √(ab) = √a · √b.

questions.prompt: Compare without a calculator. Move each coefficient under the radical, then compare: (a) $3\sqrt{5}$ and $2\sqrt{11}$; (b) $2\sqrt[3]{3}$ and $3\sqrt[3]{2}$.

responses.label: (a) Which is larger?
options: It cannot be decided without a calculator

responses.label: (b) Which is larger?
options: It cannot be decided without a calculator

hints: Moving a coefficient a under a square root squares it: a√b = √(a²b).
Under a cube root it is cubed: a∛b = ∛(a³b).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To move a coefficient a inside a square root, a√b becomes…

solutionReview.headline: Same index, so compare radicands.
solutionReview.commonError: Moving a coefficient under a root without raising it to the index: 3√5 = √(9 · 5), and 2∛3 = ∛(8 · 3).

questions.prompt: Modeling: the golden ratio. A rectangle is "golden" when its length divided by its width is $\varphi = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$, a ratio artists and architects have used for centuries. Work with $\varphi$ exactly.
hints: Square the numerator 1 + √5 and the denominator 2 separately.
For 1/φ = 2/(1 + √5), multiply by the conjugate of 1 + √5.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. ((1 + √5)/2)² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Simplify exactly; the golden ratio’s identities fall out.
solutionReview.commonError: Squaring the numerator but not the denominator: φ² = (1 + √5)²/4, not (1 + √5)²/2.

questions.prompt: Same value, different forms. Sort each expression by its simplest radical form.
hints: Simplify each expression completely before you sort it.
Rationalize any radical in a denominator first.

solutionReview.headline: Simplify each card completely, then match.
solutionReview.commonError: 6/√2 is not 6√2: rationalizing gives 6√2/2, and the 2 divides out, leaving 3√2.

sections.title: Practice — Simplest Radical Form and Beyond

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{ {{R}} x^{ {{ex}} } y^{ {{ey}} } }$. The variable $x$ can be any real number.
hints: Split {{R}} and each power into a perfect square times what is left.
x^{{ex}} = (x^{{u}})². Can x^{{u}} be negative?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For an even index n, ⁿ√(aⁿ) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Pull out the squares; mind the sign.
reasoning: √(({{s}}x^{{u}}y^{{v}})²) = {{s}}|x^{{u}}|y^{{v}}: y ≥ 0 because y is under the radical, but x^{{u}} may be negative.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving off the bars: x^{{u}} is negative whenever x is.

questions.prompt: Rationalize the denominator and simplify: $\dfrac{ {{c}} }{ {{a}} + \sqrt{ {{b}} } }$.

responses.label: After multiplying by the conjugate, the denominator is

hints: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
Simplify the fraction at the end.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To clear a binomial with a radical from a denominator, multiply the numerator and the denominator by…
options: the conjugate: the same two terms with the sign between them changed
scaffold.correct: the conjugate: the same two terms with the sign between them changed

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate, then reduce.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by the same binomial instead of its conjugate: a + √b needs a − √b to clear the radical.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2}}$.
hints: Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator.
The denominator becomes a difference of two whole numbers.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √3 · √2 equals…

solutionReview.headline: Conjugate of the denominator; FOIL the numerator.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate: the numerator is multiplied by the same factor.

questions.prompt: Simplify: $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt[3]{2}}$ and $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{4x^2}}$.
hints: Multiply 4/∛2 by the cube root that makes 2 a perfect cube.
For the second, make the denominator 8x³.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which number times 2 makes a perfect cube?

solutionReview.headline: Complete the perfect cube in each denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by ∛2/∛2: that leaves ∛4 in the denominator; a cube root needs a perfect cube, ∛8.

questions.prompt: Expand and simplify: $({{a}} + \sqrt{ {{b}} })^2$.
hints: (u + v)² = u² + 2uv + v².
Squaring √{{b}} removes the radical.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (u + v)² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Square the binomial; combine the whole numbers.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing {{a2}} + {{b}}: the middle term 2 · {{a}} · √{{b}} is part of the square.

questions.prompt: Simplify: $\sqrt[6]{64x^8y^{13}}$ and $\sqrt[3]{-54a^7}$.
hints: Split 64, x⁸ and y¹³ into sixth powers times what is left.
An odd root keeps the sign of the radicand.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. ⁶√(x⁶) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Even index: watch the bars. Odd index: keep the sign.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving off the bars in the sixth root: an even root of x⁶ is |x|, while y² is never negative.

questions.prompt: Simplify: ${{a|coef}}\sqrt{ {{P}} } + {{c|coef}}\sqrt{ {{Q}} } - {{d|coef}}\sqrt{ {{S}} }$
hints: Simplify each radical first: find the largest perfect-square factor of each radicand.
Combine like radicals by adding their coefficients.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which radicals can be combined by adding coefficients?
options: Like radicals: the same index and the same radicand
scaffold.correct: Like radicals: the same index and the same radicand

solutionReview.headline: Simplify, then combine like radicals.
solutionReview.commonError: Combining before simplifying: only like radicals combine, so simplify every radical first.

abs(a * p + c * q - d * r) != 1

questions.prompt: For $x\ge0$, what is the value of $\sqrt{{{a2}}x}\cdot\sqrt{x}$ when $x={{xval}}$?

solutionReview.headline: Multiply under one radical, then simplify.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing √x · √x as x²: √x · √x = x.

attemptFeedback: Use the algebraic structure of the expression and preserve equivalence.
supportHints: Combine like terms, distribute, factor, or simplify the radical structure as appropriate.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For x ≥ 0, √(a²x) · √x equals…

questions.prompt: Show that $3 - \sqrt{5}$ is a zero of $f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 4$, then find the other zero.
hints: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
Irrational zeros of a polynomial with integer coefficients come in conjugate pairs.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (a − b)² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute and simplify; the conjugate is the other zero.
reasoning: The conjugate 3 + √5 is the other zero: the zeros add to 6 and multiply to 9 − 5 = 4.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 3 − √5 again for the other zero: its partner is the conjugate, 3 + √5.

questions.prompt: Find positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $\sqrt{11 + 6\sqrt{2}} = a + \sqrt{b}$.
hints: Expand (a + √b)².
Match the radical parts first, then check the whole-number parts.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (a + √b)² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Square, then match the parts.
solutionReview.commonError: Reading a = 11 and b = 6√2 off the inside: square a + √b and match the parts instead.

questions.prompt: No calculator: order $4\sqrt{3}$, $3\sqrt{5}$ and $2\sqrt{11}$ from least to greatest.
hints: Move each coefficient under its radical by squaring it.
Compare the radicands.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. If 0 < u < v, then…

solutionReview.headline: Same index, so compare radicands.
reasoning: Square roots keep the order of their radicands: √44 < √45 < √48.
solutionReview.commonError: Comparing the radicands alone: 2√11 has the largest radicand but is the smallest number.

questions.prompt: For $x>0$, what is the value of $\dfrac{\sqrt{{{a2}}x^5}}{\sqrt{x}}$ when $x={{xval}}$?

solutionReview.headline: Divide under one radical, then simplify.
solutionReview.commonError: Dropping the coefficient: √{{a2}} = {{a}} still multiplies x².

attemptFeedback: Use the algebraic structure of the expression and preserve equivalence.
supportHints: Combine like terms, distribute, factor, or simplify the radical structure as appropriate.

questions.prompt: Modeling: Heron’s formula. A triangular garden has sides 5 m, 6 m and 7 m. Heron’s formula gives its area: $A = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$, where $s$ is half the perimeter. Give the exact area.

responses.label: Area in simplest radical form (square meters)

hints: Half the perimeter: add the three sides and divide by 2.
Find the largest perfect-square factor of the product.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In Heron’s formula, s is…

solutionReview.headline: Substitute, multiply, simplify the radical.
solutionReview.commonError: Using the whole perimeter for s: s is half the perimeter, 9, not 18.

questions.prompt: Error analysis. Ana simplified $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}}$ as $\dfrac{4(\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2})}{4} = \sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}$. Find her error and fix it.

responses.label: What did Ana do wrong?
options: She multiplied by √6 − √2 instead of its conjugate √6 + √2, and (√6 − √2)² is not 4
She forgot to square the numerator
responses.answer: She multiplied by √6 − √2 instead of its conjugate √6 + √2, and (√6 − √2)² is not 4

hints: A conjugate changes the sign between the two terms.
(√6 − √2)² = 6 − 2√12 + 2, which still contains a radical.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Multiplying by a conjugate works because (u − v)(u + v) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Use the conjugate, not the same binomial.
reasoning: Ana multiplied by (√6 − √2)/(√6 − √2); (√6 − √2)² = 8 − 4√3, not 4, so her denominator still has a radical.
solutionReview.commonError: (√6 − √2)² is not 6 − 2: only the conjugate product (√6 − √2)(√6 + √2) clears the radicals.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{ {{R}} m^{ {{em}} } n^{ {{en}} } }$. The variable $m$ can be any real number.

solutionReview.headline: Pull out the squares; mind the sign.
reasoning: √(({{s}}m^{{u}}n^{{v}})²) = {{s}}|m^{{u}}|n^{{v}}: n ≥ 0 because n is under the radical, but m^{{u}} may be negative.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving off the absolute value bars: m can be negative, and √(m²) = |m|.

questions.prompt: Rationalize the denominator and simplify: $\dfrac{ {{c}} }{ \sqrt{ {{b}} } - {{a}} }$.

solutionReview.headline: Multiply by the conjugate, then reduce.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by the same binomial instead of its conjugate: √b − a needs √b + a.

questions.prompt: Multiply and simplify: $({{a}} + {{b|coef}}\sqrt{ {{k}} })({{c}} - \sqrt{ {{k}} })$.

solutionReview.headline: FOIL, then combine the whole numbers and the like radicals.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting that √k · √k = k: the last product in the FOIL is a whole number, not a radical.
